Same licenses.
Different work.

Explore nine people at fictional Parkside. Everyone has a company Copilot license. Their habits, skills and useful outputs differ. Show what reaches leadership, what Leah still has to connect, and how Nine-67 would discover and build across the company.

The setup

Parkside’s CEO, Dana, sees Copilot adoption and a promising Sales demo. Suuchi plays Dana. Josh opens the company map and asks people to show real tasks. This is a fictional illustration, not an account of an actual client discovery.

How to present it

Josh operates the demo. Suuchi answers as Dana during the opening, then speaks as Nine-67’s CEO during discovery and the build discussion. Keep the map as the audience’s reference. Open one workspace at a time. Company-wide discovery comes before a focused pilot.

0:00 - 0:45 · Scene 1Open scene 1

What the CEO sees.

Josh: Introduce Parkside and invite Suuchi to answer as Dana.

Suuchi, as Dana: “I feel pretty good about where we are. Everyone has Copilot. Sales showed me something impressive. IT built an assistant for everyone. And I use Claude before board meetings.”

Josh: “If I spent a morning sitting beside your employees, what do you think I’d see?”

A license tells us what is available. It does not tell us what each person does with it or which work improves.

0:45 - 1:15 · Scene 2Open scene 2

The research gives us a reason to look.

Josh: Keep this to thirty seconds. Read the meaning of the figures, not every source detail.

“People are getting real value from AI. Miro found 83% agreeing that individuals are more productive, while 69% said most AI work happens in private sessions. Atlassian found 85% using AI at work, but 29% with it embedded in their workflow.”

“So let’s look past the licenses and see the work.”

These are separate, vendor-sponsored surveys, not a measurement of Parkside or Nine-67 results.

1:15 - 4:00 · Scene 3Open scene 3

Walk the fragmented company map.

Josh: Open the nine people from the map. For each, identify the task, the useful result and where the result stops. Do not treat every node as another chatbot demo.

  1. Dana · CEO“Dana uses Claude to challenge an approved board deck. It helps her think. She also sees Copilot adoption and Ben’s successful demo, so she assumes the company is progressing.”
  2. Daniel · IT“Daniel built AskParkside in Teams. It finds the license request form and the approver. He sees usage, but has limited visibility into which work improves.”
  3. Ben · Sales“Ben compares four weekly HubSpot exports with Copilot in Excel. He checks repeated date slips and missing buyer activity, then coaches three reps. The method largely stays in Sales.”
  4. Priya · Finance“Priya used approved Claude and synthetic rows to help write a Power Query transformation. Refresh now normalizes three branch files and flags duplicates and unmatched items for her review. Another office still does that work manually.”
  5. Nina · Operations“Nina’s team built a workflow with Teams, Power Automate and a SharePoint list. Six people use it to group reopened cases for their morning review. IT has not seen this local solution.”
  6. Marcus · Account Management“Marcus rehearses a difficult conversation in personal Grok on his phone, without names or client details. He is unsure about policy and keeps the technique to himself.”
  7. Ava · Customer Service“Ava uses Copilot twenty times a day for tone. To answer a customer, she still opens six tickets to reconstruct the context.”
  8. Elena · Project Coordination“Elena tried ‘help with my projects’ and got a generic answer. She still copies Thursday’s tracker by hand. What she needs first may be ten minutes of coaching on that actual task.”
  9. Leah · Chief of Staff“Leah manually reconciles Friday’s updates, then uses Copilot to tighten the deck. Dana uses that deck in Claude. The drafting is faster; the reconciliation still belongs to Leah.”

Josh: “All nine have the same company license. They do not have the same experience, habits or results.”

Marcus’s rehearsal is anonymized. Priya used synthetic examples when building the query. Do not turn either into an invented data-leak story. Nina’s local success is something to inspect with her and IT, not automatically replace.

Refresh, Thursday, and the adoption report.

Josh: Compare Priya’s repeatable Refresh process with Elena’s manual Thursday tracker and the Copilot adoption information Dana receives.

“Priya presses Refresh, then reviews the flagged exceptions. Elena still assembles Thursday’s tracker manually. Dana sees that both have Copilot.”

“Those three views can all be accurate. They tell very different stories about how work gets done.”

Suuchi, as Dana: “The adoption report would not have shown me that difference.”

Do not imply that Priya’s query is autonomous financial judgment. It prepares and flags data for her review. Elena’s next step may be coaching, not a new application.

5:10 - 6:00 · Scene 5Open scene 5

What actually reaches Dana?

Josh: Compare the approved work people produced with what survives into the leadership update. Dana’s Claude session receives the deck, not everyone’s private history.

“The CEO receives a cleaner report. The useful method, the source context and the cross-department relationship do not necessarily travel with it.”

Suuchi, as Dana: “Claude helps me challenge the report. Someone still has to find the evidence behind it.”

AI is not expected to know records or private conversations it has never been given. The issue is how approved business information reaches the decision.

6:00 - 7:00 · Scene 6Open scene 6

Leah still assembles the company’s story.

Josh: Show Leah’s Friday reconciliation before Copilot tightens the deck. Point to source checking, overlapping updates and missing ownership.

Josh, quoting Leah: “Everyone gets their update to me faster now. I still spend Friday figuring out which updates are talking about the same thing.”

“In this example, Leah spends two hours reconciling the updates. A better-written deck does not remove that work.”

The two hours are a fictional scenario detail, not a measured saving or a claim about all chiefs of staff.

7:00 - 8:30 · Scene 7Open scene 7

Connect the map after understanding the work.

Suuchi, as Dana: “If I brought Nine-67 in on Monday, what would you actually do?”

Josh: Switch to the connected design. Follow the approved business outputs and the people who need them. Explain the difference between a proposed connection and a live integration.

“First, we look across the company. We sit with people, inspect the work they can share, and map the tools, skills, decisions and handoffs.”

“Some opportunities are teaching. Some are reusing something a team already built. Some need a connection between business systems. We prioritize those with leadership before choosing the first build.”

Suuchi, as Nine-67’s CEO: “These connections carry approved business outputs, source links and decisions. They do not collect everyone’s private AI chats. This is a simulated design of what we could build with the right access and owners.”

Company-wide discovery does not mean one unrestricted AI that can see everything. Use scoped sources, explicit ownership and human review.

8:30 - 10:50 · Scene 8Open scene 8

Show one reviewed connection in action.

Josh: Run the service-to-account pilot. Keep the audience focused on the finding, decision, owner and progress.

  1. Review“Eight cases are proposed as related. The service manager checks the sources and excludes one unrelated address issue. Seven reviewed cases affect three accounts.”
  2. Assign“Nina receives the reviewed issue with the evidence and a Tuesday update date. The finding now has an accountable owner.”
  3. Act on the account“Marcus sees the permitted account context, owner and due date in the CRM. He adds a business observation from his customer follow-up. His private Grok session is not imported.”
  4. Keep leadership current“Nina’s progress reaches the weekly review. Leah can see the issue, its owner and what changed without assembling the same story from scratch.”

Suuchi: “The manager decides which cases belong together. Nina owns the follow-through. Marcus owns the account conversation. The workflow keeps their approved work connected.”

Eight candidates become seven reviewed cases. The root cause is not declared proven and the issue is not called resolved. Every integration and update in this demonstration is simulated.

Discover. Prioritize. Build. Measure.

Q&A: what the company map represents

The fragmented map shows fictional local practices and manual handoffs. The connected map is a proposed design: approved outputs are matched to permitted records, accountable owners and review steps. It does not depict a live deployment, automatic access to private chat histories or proof that every possible connection is worth building.

Discovery identifies what to teach, reuse, connect and build. Keep people’s useful work visible. Access, feasibility, ownership and a measurable business need determine what should move into a pilot.

Q&A: what to measure

Agree on a baseline with the owners. Measures might include time chasing inputs, repeated reconciliation, finding-to-action time, missing ownership and continued use. Choose measures that match the pilot. Do not turn the fictional Friday time or case counts into a claimed saving.

The demonstration does not provide measured ROI or a production integration result.

Research and demonstration boundaries

Miro: State of Intelligent Collaboration 2026 supplies the 83% and 69% findings. Atlassian: State of Teams 2026 supplies the 85% and 29% findings. These are self-reported vendor surveys from different samples.

Parkside, its employees, workspaces and cases are fictional. All nine featured employees have company Copilot licenses, but use different tools and methods. AI outputs, approvals, CRM writes, assignments and weekly-review updates are simulated. No private chat or live business record is accessed by this demonstration.

Josh Lee hosts and operates the demo. Suuchi Ramesh plays Dana, Parkside’s fictional CEO, then explains Nine-67’s approach. The AI Workflow Discovery Session follows the webinar.
